name: Slate
lede: Slate is the blue-tinted grey of the roofing stone, a color word that books define as dark, mid or bluish and that has spread into a family of twenty-one names.

sections.title: A rock, then a shade
sections.body:
Slate is a rock before it is a color: a fine-grained metamorphosed mudstone or shale that splits into thin sheets, and the Pigment Compendium stresses that the word does not name any one mineral [1]. The stone and its uses have their own page at [[slate-grey]]. This page follows the word as it spreads through the color system.

Books disagree about what the color is. Paterson defines slate as a dark bluish grey but slate grey as simply a dark grey [6]. St Clair's glossary calls it a mid-azure grey [7]. Eckstut groups slate with sky blue as a shade rather than a hue: it tells you how dark and dull a blue is, not which hue it is [8].

The web swatch, #708090, is the X11 color SlateGray [6]. Other picks for slate run darker. The xkcd survey's two slates and the paint standard RAL 7015 sit at a lightness of 36 to 42 on the CIELAB scale, against 53 for the web swatch [12].

sections.title: A family of slates
sections.body:
Our library holds 21 names with slate in them, most from Ridgway's plates of 1912 [12]. They drift away from grey in every direction: [[slate-purple]], Slate-Olive, [[slate-green]], Violet-Slate, Heliotrope-Slate and Vinaceous-Slate among them [12]. The X11 SlateBlue, #6A5ACD, is a violet-blue and not grey at all [6]. [[medium-slate-blue]] is its lighter cousin on the web [12].

Syme's table shows the same looseness in the rock itself [9]. His mineral example for Greenish Grey is clay slate, together with wacke, a sandstone [9]. In his table, then, the rock sits with the greenish greys rather than the blue ones.

sections.title: In the paint box
sections.body:
Slate has been ground for paint, though never as a prized pigment. In 1896 Winsor & Newton listed Davy's grey, a new color prepared from a special variety of slate and suggested by a Mr. Henry Davy [2]. By 1928 Heaton recorded the name as a variety of slate powder [2]. The same ground rock lies behind the old name mineral grey, but books disagree: Field and later editors called it an inferior ultramarine ash, while Martel in 1860 identified it as finely levigated slate [3].

Slate black was made by calcining a bituminous shale, which gave a black with about 15 per cent carbon, and the same source says Spanish black could mean slate black as well as the usual cork char [1][5]. Prince's metallic brown is a grey rock turned brown by fire: its ore was bluish grey when mined, and roasting converted it to an oxide [4]. Its original maker, Robert Prince of New York, came to it through a slate quarry in Carbon County, Pennsylvania [4].

Slate has also been a surface. Anish Kapoor's *A Wing at the Heart of Things*, from 1990, is slate coated in [[prussian-blue]] [11]. Birren, collecting notes from older medical literature, lists slate as a skin color in argyria and in Addison's disease [10].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of #708090 covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 331 works, 1.4 per cent [13]. It leans modern. The 1900s carry it at 3.5 per cent, 2.5 times the archive rate, and the 1920s peak at 11 of 237 paintings, 4.6 per cent [13]. None of the 443 works from before 1400 has it, and the first dated example is Spinello Aretino's *Virgin and Child with Angels* of about 1405 [13].

[[painter:claude-monet|Monet]] has it in 6 of his 50 paintings here, about 9 times the archive rate, and Philips Wouwerman in 5 of 36 [13]. [[look:impressionism|Impressionism]] carries it 5.1 times as often as the archive average [13]. The largest areas are storm water and an Indian court scene [13]. [[painting:smk-KMS3767|Eckersberg's privateer outsailing a frigate]] from 1845 is 50 per cent this color, [[painting:cma-170085|a portrait of Shamsher Sen of Mandi]] from about 1760 is 50 per cent, and [[painting:smk-KMS405|Melbye's Shetland fishing boat in a storm]] from 1842 is 49 per cent [13].

In half of the paintings that carry it, it sits in the mid-tones [13]. It most often shares a canvas with [[denim]], 5 times the usual rate, then grey and [[charcoal]] [13]. In Google Books the word *slate* peaks around 1841 and falls to about 30 per cent of that level by 2000, though the count includes every sense of the word, from roofs to writing boards [14]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [13].

questions.q: What was the paint Winsor & Newton listed in 1896 as Davy's grey made from?
Why do books describe slate as such different greys, from mid to dark and from azure to plain?
choices: Slate names a rock type, not one mineral, so its color varies
Slate was only named in the twentieth century
Slate is always black when freshly cut
A single standard fixes its color
questions.answer: Slate names a rock type, not one mineral, so its color varies

questions.q: The X11 color SlateBlue is a grey.

openers: Winsor & Newton sold a grey ground from slate in 1896 and called it Davy's grey.
The web's SlateBlue is a violet-blue, nothing like the grey of a roof.
Prince's metallic brown began as a bluish-grey rock that turned brown in the kiln.
